## 5. Modifier surface

Properties, value types, and emission rules come from
[MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md); the tables here give the **DSL signature**. A
compound SwiftUI modifier expands to **one `SET_PROPERTY` per underlying
property** (`.frame` → `WIDTH` + `HEIGHT` + `ALIGNMENT`; `.border` →
`BORDER_COLOR` + `BORDER_WIDTH`; `.shadow` → `SHADOW_COLOR` + `SHADOW_RADIUS` +
`SHADOW_X` + `SHADOW_Y`). The `Java DSL` column is the reference realization.

### 5.0 Authoring a modifier

**One mechanism for every modifier.** Each entry below is a `ViewModifier`
value, applied through the shared `modifiers(...)` operation:

- **Parameterized modifiers** are created with `modifierName(c -> …)` (a fluent
  config builder), e.g. `padding(p -> p.uniform(16))`,
  `frame(f -> f.width(100).height(24))`.
- **Single-value modifiers** — a font, a font weight, an alignment, a style —
  may pass the value directly, because the value type *is* the modifier: `FontWeight.BOLD`,
  `TextAlignment.CENTER`, `Font.headline()`, `MyButtonStyle`.
- A modifier's type is **never** suffixed with `Mod` (§1).

```java
Text.make(t -> t.text("hi")).modifiers(
        padding(p -> p.uniform(16)),
        frame(f -> f.width(100).height(24)),
        FontWeight.BOLD,
        foregroundStyle(f -> f.color(Color.WHITE)));
```

**Every value member above also accepts a `Signal<T>`**
(`padding(p -> p.uniform(padSignal))`, `frame(f -> f.width(widthSignal))`,
`foregroundStyle(f -> f.color(colorSignal))`) — see
[§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation). Because `Signal<T>` is a
`@FunctionalInterface`, a bare lambda would also type-check but would register a
(harmless) reactive binding; **literals MUST use the raw overload**, which wraps
a `ConstantSignal` (no binding overhead).

### 5.1 Layout & frame

| Modifier | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Java DSL | Property(ies) |
|----------|---------------------------|----------|---------------|
| `frame` | `.frame(width:height:alignment:)` | `.modifiers(frame(f -> f.width(w).height(h).alignment(a)))` — the 2D `Alignment` positions the content within the box; omitted → no `ALIGNMENT` emitted, a stack's own alignment is preserved | `WIDTH` 0x100B, `HEIGHT` 0x100C, `ALIGNMENT` 0x0002 (only when provided) |
| `frame(min:…)` | `.frame(minWidth:idealWidth:maxWidth:minHeight:idealHeight:maxHeight:)` | `.modifiers(frame(f -> f.minWidth(..).idealWidth(..).maxWidth(..).minHeight(..).idealHeight(..).maxHeight(..)))` (the `Frame.Builder`; unset bounds are omitted — NaN/∞ = no limit) | `MIN_WIDTH` 0x0012 … `MAX_HEIGHT` 0x0017 |
| `padding` | `.padding(_:)` / `.padding(_:edges:)` | `.modifiers(padding(p -> p.uniform(float)))` / `.modifiers(padding(p -> p.edges(t, r, b, l)))` | `PADDING` 0x1011 / `PADDING_TOP` 0x1012 … `PADDING_LEFT` 0x1015 |
| `offset` | `.offset(x:y:)` | `.modifiers(offset(o -> o.x(float).y(float)))` | `OFFSET_X` 0x000E, `OFFSET_Y` 0x000F |
| `position` | `.position(x:y:)` | `.modifiers(position(p -> p.x(float).y(float)))` | `POSITION_X` 0x0010, `POSITION_Y` 0x0011 |
| `fixedSize` | `.fixedSize()` / `.fixedSize(horizontal:vertical:)` | `.modifiers(fixedSize())` / `.modifiers(fixedSize(f -> f.horizontal(boolean).vertical(boolean)))` | `FIXED_SIZE_HORIZONTAL` 0x0018, `FIXED_SIZE_VERTICAL` 0x0019 |
| `layoutPriority` | `.layoutPriority(_:)` | `.modifiers(layoutPriority(l -> l.value(float)))` | `LAYOUT_PRIORITY` 0x001A |
| `zIndex` | `.zIndex(_:)` | `.modifiers(zIndex(z -> z.value(float)))` | `Z_INDEX` 0x100F |
| `aspectRatio` | `.aspectRatio(_:contentMode:)` | `.modifiers(aspectRatio(a -> a.ratio(float).contentMode(ContentMode)))` | `ASPECT_RATIO` 0x001B, `CONTENT_MODE` 0x001C |
| `scaledToFit` | `.scaledToFit()` | `.modifiers(scaledToFit())` | `CONTENT_MODE` 0x001C (Fit) |
| `scaledToFill` | `.scaledToFill()` | `.modifiers(scaledToFill())` | `CONTENT_MODE` 0x001C (Fill) |
| `minimumScaleFactor` | `.minimumScaleFactor(_:)` | `.modifiers(minimumScaleFactor(m -> m.value(float)))` | `MINIMUM_SCALE_FACTOR` 0x001D |

**Semantics**: `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` use the sentinels `FILL` (−1.0 = expand) and
`HUG_CONTENT` (−2.0 = intrinsic); omitting an axis leaves it to the native
renderer. SwiftUI's `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` / `maxHeight: .infinity` is
written by passing `Float.POSITIVE_INFINITY` (Java) / `f32::INFINITY` (Rust) to
the width/height builder members, which is normalized to `FILL` before emission.
In the min/ideal/max builder an infinite `maxWidth`/`maxHeight` means *no limit*
(the bound is omitted). `OFFSET` is a post-layout translation; `POSITION` is
absolute placement within the parent.

signal change re-emits only that `META::SET_WINDOW_METADATA` field; the renderer
maps it to the window/tab title and description.

### 5.6 Custom modifiers (developer-authored)

In SwiftUI any developer can define a modifier that applies to **any** existing
view — and Pathland is the same. This is a **first-class, MUST** property of
every conformant DSL: modifiers are never hard-bound to a view type.

- **Applicable to any view.** A modifier works on a library primitive
  (`Text`), a container (`VStack`), a control (`Button`), a custom view, or an
  already-modified view. The same modifier value applies everywhere.
- **One mechanism.** Core and application-authored modifiers are the **same
  surface**: a `ViewModifier` value applied via `.modifiers(...)`. There is
  **no per-modifier sugar on the view type**; a parameterized modifier is
  constructed by a lowercase static function named for the modifier ([§5.0](#50-authoring-a-modifier))
  and single-value modifiers pass the value directly.

| | Canonical | Java DSL (`com.pathland.view`) | Rust DSL (`pathland-view`) |
|-|-----------|-------------------------------|----------------------------|
| authoring | `struct Card: ViewModifier { func body(content: Content) -> some View }` | `@FunctionalInterface ViewModifier { View body(View content) }` | `trait ViewModifier { fn apply(&mut Node) }` |
| applying | `content.modifier(Card())` | `content.modifiers(card(c -> …))` / `content.modifiers(A, B)` | `content.modifiers(Card)` |
| single-value | `.modifier(Padding(16))` | `content.modifiers(padding(p -> p.uniform(16)))` | `content.modifiers(Padding(16.0))` |

**Composition**: a custom modifier composes core modifiers **or** wraps
`content` with additional structure (a background, an overlay, a frame) and
returns the decorated view — exactly SwiftUI's `body(content: Content)`.

**Emission contract**: a custom modifier composed from core modifiers emits the
same one-`SET_PROPERTY`-per-property deltas as writing the modifiers inline;
emission stays diff-based, and a renderer that cannot apply a modifier
**allows and ignores** it.

**Realization deltas**:
- **Rust** — every core modifier (`Padding`, `FontSize`, `ForegroundStyle`,
  `Frame`, …) implements `ViewModifier`, and `.modifiers(...)` applies them
  (a single modifier or a tuple).
  Caveat: `apply(&mut Node)` mutates the built node's properties only — it
  cannot wrap `content` with new structure (the Java/SwiftUI `body(content)`
  form can). A conformant DSL's custom-modifier mechanism should support
  wrapping.
- **Java** — every core modifier is a `ViewModifier` value applied via
  `.modifiers(...)`; `View` has no modifier sugar, and a style
  (`ButtonStyle`, …) is itself a `ViewModifier` value (it binds the
  `Environment.BUTTON_STYLE` key down the subtree — subtree scoping is
  environment-only). Application-authored `ViewModifier.body(View)` is
  SwiftUI-shaped and can wrap content with structure.

#### Media (`MediaController`)

A media playback is a **state object**, not a view (spec/MEDIA.md; the SwiftUI
`AVPlayer` analog). `MediaController` owns the transport as signals — commands
(`source()`, `playing()`, `position()`, `volume()`, `muted()`, `loop()`,
`rate()`) and reports (`time()`, `duration()`, `volumeReport()`) — plus
`play()/pause()/toggle()/seek()/setVolume()`. The emitter materializes one
non-visual `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` node per controller (keyed by object identity), so
playback is stable across structural swaps.

- **Audio has no view**: bind ordinary views (buttons/sliders) to the
  controller's signals. Include `controller.attach()` once in the tree — a
  non-visual marker that materializes the controller node — placed **outside**
  any swapping branch (e.g. a `SizeThatFits` slot).
- **Video** is the only media view: `Video.make(controller)` renders the
  controller's output. `VideoStyle` supplies a custom control surface; the
  default `NativeVideoStyle` shows renderer-native controls.
- A `MediaController` may be rebound to the app's own (e.g. persisted) signals
  (`controller.playing(signal)`), so the controller drives the same state the
  rest of the UI reads.

```java
MediaController player = new MediaController(computed(() -> track.get().audio()));
player.playing(playing.signal()).position(seekRequest.signal()).volume(volume.signal());
player.time(position.signal()).onEnded(this::next);

VStack.make().children(
    player.attach(),                                   // audio: non-visual
    Button.make(b -> b.action(player::toggle)),
    Slider.make(s -> s.value(player.time())),
    Video.make(player));                               // video: the only media view
```

## 5.7 Styleable controls (the style contract)

A **style** customizes a view or control's *content*; the control owns its
*component and interaction*. This is one contract for every styleable surface
(`ButtonStyle`, `LabelStyle`, `VideoStyle`, …), and it is the
author-facing shape of the protocol's **Composite Override Mode**
([PRIMITIVES.md §2](./PRIMITIVES.md#2-dual-mode-rendering-pipeline--platform-delegation)).

- **The control owns the native component and the interaction.** A semantic
  control renders its **native control node** (its component id — `BUTTON`,
  `VIDEO`, …) and attaches its behavior to *that* node: the tap action /
  `EVENT_LISTENERS` (Button), the value/text/date sink, or the media binding
  (`Video`). The **whole control is interactive**, including its padding.
- **The style owns the content.** A style returns the control's **content view**
  from `makeBody(Config)`; the control attaches it as the control node's
  **single child**. The content keeps its own component(s), layout, and
  properties — a style **never** sets or overwrites the control's component and
  never wires the interaction. The result is a control with children → protocol
  **Composite Override Mode**.
- **The style consumes the control's config.** The `Config` a style's
  `makeBody(Config)` receives is the **same type** the view configured through
  `make(...)` ([§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation)): `ButtonStyle.makeBody(Button.Config)`,
  `LabelStyle.makeBody(Label.Config)`,
  `VideoStyle.makeBody(VideoStyle.Configuration)`. The style **reads** the config (the
  control's values: content, action, label, media state); it does not mutate it.
- **A style is a modifier.** Styles are `ViewModifier` values scoped down a
  subtree with `.modifiers(<Style>)`, binding the style's `EnvironmentKey` over
  the wrapped subtree (nearest wins); the control reads it via its
  `Environment.<name>Style()` accessor. This is the one inheritance mechanism
  ([§6 rule 6](#6-authoring-conventions)); `ButtonStyle` binds
  `Environment.BUTTON_STYLE`, `VideoStyle` `Environment.VIDEO_STYLE`, `LabelStyle`
  `Environment.LABEL_STYLE`.
- **Button content precedence (three developer options).** A `Button`'s content
  resolves as: (1) an **explicit child** supplied via `.children(...)` wins;
  else (2) the config **title** string (wrapped as a `Text`); else (3) the
  **style-supplied content** from `makeBody`. The `buttonStyle` modifier itself
  (option 3) lets a developer hand content in through the style. This mirrors
  SwiftUI's multiple button-authoring forms.
- **Defaults preserve the native path.** The default style contributes the
  control's natural content: `PlainButtonStyle` → the label;
  `NativeVideoStyle` → **no content** (an empty-content
  sentinel), so the control stays a **leaf** in Native Token Mode and the
  renderer shows native media controls; `DefaultLabelStyle` → title + icon.
- **Text/foreground modifiers cascade to content.** A `.foregroundStyle`/
  `.fontSize` (and the other inherited text modifiers) applied *to the control*
  reach the content's text — SwiftUI environment semantics. In the Java DSL the
  properties ride the control node; renderers cascade them to child text.
- **Main-axis alignment is the content's own layout — no protocol property.**
  A control's content box centers its child by default; to left-align a
  composite label (e.g. a navigation row), make the label full-width
  (`frame(f -> f.width(FILL))`) and let its own `ALIGNMENT` place its
  content. There is deliberately no main-axis/justification property (the engine
  describes WHAT, never WHERE — [§1](#1-design-principles-dsl-flavored)).
- **Closed-variant ("token") styles are the same surface, not a wrapper.** Some
  styles select a whole native variant rather than supplying content:
  `ToggleStyle`/`PickerStyle`/`TextStyle` are wire **enums** applied as
  properties (`TOGGLE_STYLE`, …), and `LabelStyle` shapes which parts render.
  They are scoped/read exactly like the wrapper styles above.

Canonical signatures (SwiftUI-shaped) and the realization:

| Control | Style protocol | `Config` | Default style |
|---------|----------------|----------|---------------|
| `Button` | `ButtonStyle { makeBody(config) -> View }` | the `Button.Config` (title, action, content) | `PlainButtonStyle` (label) |
| `Label` | `LabelStyle { makeBody(config) -> View }` | the `Label.Config` (title, icon) | `DefaultLabelStyle` (title + icon) |
| `Video` | `VideoStyle { makeBody(config) -> View }` | the `VideoStyle.Configuration` (its `MediaController`) | `NativeVideoStyle` (no content) |

```java
// Button: the control wires the action; the style decorates the label/content.
enum MyButtonStyle implements ButtonStyle { INSTANCE;
    @Override public View makeBody(Button.Config c) {
        return c.content().modifiers(padding(p -> p.uniform(12)), background(b -> b.color(BLUE)));
    }
}
Button.make(b -> b.title("Save").action(this::save)).modifiers(MyButtonStyle.INSTANCE);

// Label: the style decides which parts render (nullable parts = absent).
enum BadgeLabelStyle implements LabelStyle { INSTANCE;
    @Override public View makeBody(Label.Config c) {
        return HStack.make().children(
                c.icon().modifiers(frame(f -> f.width(18).height(18))),
                c.title());
    }
}
```

The Java DSL ships `PlainButtonStyle`/`BorderedButtonStyle`,
`DefaultLabelStyle`/`TitleOnlyLabelStyle`/`IconOnlyLabelStyle`, and
`NativeVideoStyle`; application-authored styles implement the
same interfaces. **Delta:** SwiftUI's `LabelStyleConfiguration.title`/`.icon`
are always-present views; Pathland passes `null` for an absent part (a style
checks `hasTitle()`/`hasIcon()`). Because styles are modifiers, a style is
applied with `.modifiers(<Style>)`.

## 6. Authoring conventions

A conformant DSL follows these conventions:

1. **Names**: SwiftUI view/modifier names; per-language case (camelCase,
   snake_case). `foregroundStyle` not `foregroundColor`; `fontWeight`,
   `multilineTextAlignment`, `scaledToFit`, `allowsHitTesting` keep their
   SwiftUI spellings. A modifier's type is **never** suffixed `Mod`.
2. **Signature order**: canonical parameter order is preserved —
   `.border(color, width)`, `.frame(width, height, alignment)`,
   `.shadow(color, radius, x, y)`. Compound modifiers expand to one property
   per argument.
3. **Values vs modifiers**: structural/layout values and a control's bound value
   are configured through a view's `make(...)` (modifiers through lowercase
   functions); everything else is a chainable `modifiers(...)` value. The three
   operations may be chained in any order.
4. **Typed enums**: `HorizontalAlignment` (leading/center/trailing, for
   `VStack`), `VerticalAlignment` (top/center/bottom, for `HStack`), `Alignment`
   (2D — topLeading … bottomTrailing — for `ZStack`/grids and the `frame`
   modifier's content alignment); all **position-only, never stretching** (a
   child's `FILL` size kind stretches). Plus `TextAlignment`, `FontWeight`
   (100–900), `Truncation` (head/middle/tail),
   `TextCase` (none/uppercase/lowercase), `FontStyle` (normal/italic),
   `FontDesign` (default/serif/rounded/monospaced), `ContentMode` (fit/fill),
   `ControlSize` (small/regular/large), `ToggleStyle`
   (switch/checkbox/button), `PickerStyle` (menu/segmented/wheel/radiogroup),
   `DatePickerMode` (date/time/dateAndTime), `ShapeKind`
   (circle/rectangle/roundedRectangle/capsule/ellipse/path). Numeric codes
   come from MODIFIERS.md's appendix; the DSL resolves them.
5. **`Spacer`/`Color` as views**: `Spacer` is a flexible expanding filler;
   `Color` in a tree is a layout-greedy fill.
6. **The environment is the only inheritance mechanism.** Any value that must
   reach a whole subtree — a style (`ButtonStyle`), the router, the active path,
   the session's persisted state — is injected through the environment, never
   threaded through constructors and never through a second scoping system. The
   environment is a hierarchical, nearest-wins scope of typed `EnvironmentKey`
   values (the `EnvironmentBinding` modifier value / `Environment.value(key)`,
   Java; §4.5). A language MAY implement the scope with a thread-local over the
   synchronous render pass (Java does) — but that is the implementation of the
   one mechanism, not an additional one. A subtree-scoping modifier MUST be
   expressed as an `EnvironmentKey` binding: `ButtonStyle` binds
   `Environment.BUTTON_STYLE` (`EnvironmentKey<ButtonStyle>`), exactly like the
   router and the active path.
7. **Reactivity discipline**: `body()` is a tracked render; a signal read there
   subscribes the component and a later write re-renders that component, whose
   subtree is diffed into deltas. A bound node stays fine-grained (one delta, no
   body re-run). Never write signals during render. Non-signal reads are
   mount-time only ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-reactive-bodies--slots)).
8. **Emission contract**: each DSL call emits exactly the documented
   properties with the documented value types; the emitter diffs. The DSL never
   computes layout, never positions, never serializes full trees.

---

## 7. Theme management

Pathland theming is **application-owned over a renderer-owned token system**
([TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md); the wire encoding lives in [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md)
§Design Token System). The DSL gives the author two distinct surfaces:

1. **Token references in style modifiers** — semantic intent instead of a
   literal: `foregroundStyle(f -> f.color(Color.token("color.primary")))`
   emits a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference the renderer resolves against the current
   scheme. No opcode is re-emitted when a token or the scheme changes.
2. **Global theme overrides** — a batch of `PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` commands
   rolled at mount: a single-scheme `Theme` or an `AdaptiveTheme` light+dark
   pair (base = **light**, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark**).

> **Ownership**: the application owns theme values (base + `dark.*`) and token
> references; the renderer owns token defaults (light + dark), effective
> color-scheme detection, resolution (override → default → parent → fallback),
> and interaction-state styling (hover/pressed/focus/disabled). The protocol
> never transmits hover/click/transition styling.

### 7.1 Token-typed values

Any property whose value type is `COLOR` / `F32` / `STRING` / `ENUM` MAY carry a
**token reference** instead of a literal value (MODIFIERS.md §Value types). The
reference rides the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`) with the token path in
the arena — **never** a packed literal. A property carries exactly one value
(literal or reference, never both).

| Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Java DSL | Rust DSL | Emits |
|----------------------------|----------|----------|-------|
| `Color.token("color.primary")` | `Color.token("color.primary")` | `Color::token("color.primary")` | `DESIGN_TOKEN` ref (`0x08`) in any COLOR-typed property: `COLOR` 0x100A (`.foregroundStyle`), `BACKGROUND_COLOR` 0x1001, `BORDER_COLOR` 0x1004, `SHADOW_COLOR` 0x1021, `TINT` 0x1030, … |
| `Color.token("dark.color.surface")` | `Color.token("dark.color.surface")` | `Color::token("dark.color.surface")` | same — an explicit dark-variant reference (resolves the dark layer in either scheme) |
| `.padding(space.2)` / `Spacing(space.2)` | `Padding.with(Length.token("space.2"))` / `spacing(Length.token("space.2"))` | `Padding(Length::token("space.2"))` / `spacing(Length::token("space.2"))` | `DESIGN_TOKEN` ref in a F32-typed property: `PADDING` 0x1011 / `SPACING` 0x0001 / `CONTENT_MARGINS` 0x0005, … (see TOKENS.md §Generative token families) |
| `Font.body.family` token | `FontFamily.token("font.body.family")` | `FontFamily::token("font.body.family")` | `DESIGN_TOKEN` ref in a STRING-typed property (`FONT_FAMILY`) |

Token references are **static paths**: a signal-bound property carries a
literal value, not a token reference.

`Color` keeps its dual identity: as a **View** it is a layout-greedy fill; as a
token reference (`Color.token(path)`) it is a **data value** passed to
style-taking modifiers. A token-typed property resolves renderer-side and
**re-resolves automatically** when the effective scheme changes — overrides and
scheme are renderer state, so no node is ever re-emitted for a theme/scheme
change.

Rules:

1. Reference any token path — the standard catalog (TOKENS.md §Standard Token
   Catalog) or an application-defined path. A renderer that cannot apply a token
   falls back rather than erroring.
2. `space.<N>` members are **generative**: reference them freely (`space.2`,
   `space.0.5`), but override only `space.base` (see §7.2 rule 2).
3. A token reference must not be combined with a literal on the same property.

### 7.2 Global theme overrides

A **theme** is a batch of token overrides. Every override defines **exactly one
value**; combine a light and a dark `Theme` via `AdaptiveTheme` for adaptive
theming.

| Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Java DSL (`com.pathland.view`) | Rust DSL (`pathland-view` / `pathland-engine`) | Emits |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-------|
| `Theme()` — one-scheme override batch | `new Theme().color(...)...` | `Theme::new()` | one `PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` per override (`A` = arena path, `B` = valueType, `C` = value) |
| `.color("color.primary", 0xFF2563EB)` | `.color("color.primary", 0xFF2563EB)` | `.color("color.primary", 0xFF2563EB)` | `COLOR`-typed override (sRGB `0xAARRGGBB`) |
| `.f32("space.base", 4.0)` | `.f32("space.base", 4.0f)` | `.f32("space.base", 4.0)` | `F32`-typed override (lengths in device pixels) |
| `.u32("…", v)` / `.u8("…", v)` | `.u32(path, int)` / `.u8(path, int)` | `.u32(path, v)` / `.u8(path, v)` | `U32` / `U8`-typed override |
| `.string("font.body.family", "Inter")` | `.string(path, String)` | `.string(path, "Inter")` | `STRING`-typed override (arena) |
| `AdaptiveTheme(light, dark)` | `new AdaptiveTheme(light, dark)` | `AdaptiveTheme::new(light, dark)` | light overrides as base tokens; dark overrides `dark.`-prefixed |

Emission contract:

- The theme is emitted **once at mount** as a frame of
  `PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` opcodes before the tree. Java: `new Emitter(sink,
  theme)` emits it at the start of the mount and `renderFull` (resync) frames;
  Rust: `Engine::apply_theme` / `Engine::apply_adaptive_theme`.
- Overrides are **renderer state**: they never re-emit nodes and never
  participate in the diff — an unchanged tree with a theme still emits **zero**
  per-node opcodes.
- `AdaptiveTheme` emits the light `Theme`'s overrides as base paths and the dark
  `Theme`'s with the `dark.` prefix (added automatically when the author wrote a
  bare path). The renderer derives the effective scheme from the platform and
  resolves each override against it.
- The renderer supplies light + dark defaults for the whole Tier 1 catalog, so
  dark mode works even when the author only overrides base tokens.

Authoring rules:

1. Override any token in the catalog or an application-defined path; never
   assume specific renderer default values.
2. Override `space.base` to control the whole spacing scale — individual
   `space.<N>` members MUST NOT be overridden.
3. Overrides are **global and renderer-wide**: apply the theme once per
   session/host at mount, not per view.

### 7.3 Runtime theming and scheme choice

A host MAY replace the theme after mount. Replacement is **reset + apply**: the
host emits `META::RESET_THEME` followed by the new theme's
`PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides in one frame. The renderer clears the
old overrides, re-resolves every token-referencing property, and re-applies the
new values; no node is re-emitted.

The host MAY also force the effective scheme with
`META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME`:

| Canonical mode | Emits | Behavior |
|----------------|-------|----------|
| `.platform` | `SET_COLOR_SCHEME` A=0 | follow the OS/browser light/dark signal (default) |
| `.light` | `SET_COLOR_SCHEME` A=1 | force the light design |
| `.dark` | `SET_COLOR_SCHEME` A=2 | force the dark design |

While forced, platform scheme changes are ignored. Returning to `.platform`
restores native detection. Both commands are renderer state — the emitter
re-resolves, never re-emitting the tree.

Java exposes this through `Emitter.replaceTheme(...)` / `resetTheme()` /
`setColorScheme(...)`; the server runtime's host-level
`PathlandSession.setTheme(...)` / `setColorScheme(...)` delegate to the same
emission path. Rust exposes `Engine::reset_theme` / `set_color_scheme` (and
`replace_theme` / `replace_adaptive_theme`).

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, 'docs/**', 'feature/**', 'fix/**', 'spec/**']
  pull_request:

jobs:
  design:
    name: Design (Style Dictionary)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node 22
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: design/package-lock.json

      # Build the generated token CSS / manifest / bundle and validate the
      # three token layers against the protocol catalog, dark/forced-dark
      # rules, and the canonical length conventions.
      - name: Install, build, check
        working-directory: design
        run: |
          npm ci
          npm run build
          npm run check

      # The Rust renderer embeds the generated bundle (committed for packaging).
      - name: Verify the committed renderer CSS matches the design build
        run: scripts/sync-design-css.sh --check

  rust:
    name: Rust (workspace + C ABI + no_std/wasm)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [design]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # The workspace includes pathland-render-gtk (GTK4 + libadwaita + GStreamer)
      # and pathland-render-qt (Qt Quick), so the runner needs the GTK4,
      # libadwaita, GStreamer, and Qt system libraries before `cargo test` can
      # link them. GStreamer is required because the GTK renderer plays app-driven
      # media through a direct GStreamer playbin (GTK4's own media backend is
      # compiled out of some builds); the plugins are the runtime set the audio
      # stack uses (playbin, volume/audioconvert, mp3 decode). The Qt libraries
      # are installed in the next step.
      - name: Install GTK4 + libadwaita + GStreamer system dependencies
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y \
            libgtk-4-dev \
            libadwaita-1-dev \
            libglib2.0-dev \
            libcairo2-dev \
            libpango1.0-dev \
            libgdk-pixbuf-2.0-dev \
            libgraphene-1.0-dev \
            libgstreamer1.0-dev \
            gstreamer1.0-plugins-base \
            gstreamer1.0-plugins-good \
            gstreamer1.0-libav

      - name: Install Qt6 (QML/Quick) system dependencies
        run: |
          sudo apt-get install -y \
            qt6-base-dev \
            qt6-declarative-dev \
            qt6-declarative-private-dev \
            qt6-multimedia-dev \
            qml6-module-qtqml \
            qml6-module-qtqml-models \
            qml6-module-qtqml-workerscript \
            qml6-module-qtquick \
            qml6-module-qtquick-layouts \
            qml6-module-qtquick-controls \
            qml6-module-qtquick-templates \
            qml6-module-qtquick-window \
            qml6-module-qtmultimedia
        # The dev headers alone don't ship the QML runtime modules; the Qt
        # renderer's offscreen tests instantiate the QML (QtQml + WorkerScript,
        # Items, stacks/Grid via QtQuick.Layouts, Qt Quick Controls, Multimedia)
        # through QQmlComponent, so the qml6-module-* runtime files are required
        # too. Note the Qt6 package names: `-window` (the Qt5 `-window2` name
        # does not exist), and private headers need qt6-declarative-private-dev.

      - name: Install Rust (stable + wasm32 target)
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          targets: wasm32-unknown-unknown

      - name: Cache cargo
        uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          workspaces: lib/rust -> target

      - name: Test workspace
        working-directory: lib/rust
        run: cargo test

      - name: Qt renderer headless smoke
        working-directory: lib/rust
        env:
          QT_QPA_PLATFORM: offscreen
          QT_QUICK_BACKEND: software
        run: cargo test -p pathland-render-qt

      # The DOM renderer's constants/token conventions and the cross-renderer SSR
      # golden fixtures are GENERATED from Rust (pathland-ts-codegen /
      # pathland-html-golden). Regenerate them here and fail if the committed
      # files drifted — so a renumbered constant or a changed SSR shape can't land
      # without its TS/fixture counterparts.
      - name: Verify generated TS + golden fixtures are current (no drift)
        working-directory: lib/rust
        run: |
          cargo run -p pathland-ts-codegen
          cargo run -p pathland-html-golden -- --emit
          git diff --exit-code -- \
            lib/typescript/src/constants.ts \
            lib/typescript/src/generated \
            lib/typescript/test/fixtures/ssr

      - name: Build the C ABI (cdylib, used by the Java JNA ring interop / native hosts)
        working-directory: lib/rust
        run: cargo build -p pathland-core-capi

      - name: no_std / wasm32 direction guard
        working-directory: lib/rust
        run: ./check-wasm.sh

      # The Java HTML renderer shim needs the Rust renderer cdylib (the jar embeds
      # it so it travels with the artifact). Build it here and hand it to the java
      # job via an artifact.
      - name: Build the HTML renderer cdylib
        working-directory: lib/rust
        run: cargo build -p pathland-render-html

      - name: Upload the renderer dylib for the java job
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: pathland-render-html-native
          path: lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_render_html.so
          retention-days: 1

  java:
    name: Java (Maven reactor, JDK ${{ matrix.java }})
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [rust]
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        java: ['17', '21', '25']
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Whole-stack floor is Java 17 (maven.compiler.release=17; JNA native binding,
      # thread-local environment); the matrix proves every LTS from 17.
      - name: Set up JDK ${{ matrix.java }}
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: ${{ matrix.java }}
          cache: maven

      # The renderer jar embeds the Rust cdylib (built by the rust job). Restore it
      # into the debug dir the jar-embed step copies.
      - name: Download the Rust renderer dylib
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: pathland-render-html-native
          path: lib/rust/target/debug

      - name: Test reactor (incl. the SSR web demos)
        working-directory: lib/java
        run: mvn -q -B test

    name: Web client (TypeScript DOM renderer)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: lib/typescript/package-lock.json

      - name: Install, typecheck, test, build
        working-directory: lib/typescript
        run: |
          npm ci
          npm run typecheck
          npm test
          npm run build

      # The demos serve the committed bundle from their static resource dirs
      # (content-hashed dom-renderer-<sha256>.js + the dom-renderer.current
      # pointer; stale hashed copies are pruned); copying the freshly built one

      - name: Verify the committed bundle matches the source (no drift)
        working-directory: lib/typescript
        run: |

          git diff --exit-code -- lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/src/main/resources lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-demo/src/main/resources

      - name: Install Playwright browsers
        working-directory: lib/typescript

## 10. Appendix A: SwiftUI ↔ DSL signature map

Representative rows; the full surface is in [§4](#4-view-surface) and
[§5](#5-modifier-surface).

| SwiftUI | Canonical DSL | Java DSL | Rust DSL |
|---------|---------------|----------|----------|
| `Text("Hi")` | `Text("Hi")` | `Text.make(t -> t.text("Hi"))` | `text("Hi")` |
| `VStack(alignment: .center, spacing: 8) { … }` | `VStack(alignment:spacing:) { … }` | `VStack.make(v -> v.alignment(Alignment.CENTER).spacing(8)).children(…)` | `VStack::with(\|v\| { v.spacing(8.0); }).children(vec![…])` |
| `Button("+") { inc() }` | `Button("+", action)` | `Button.make(b -> b.title("+").action(() -> inc()))` | `button("+")` (no action yet) |
| `TextField("Name", text: $name)` | `TextField("Name", text: writable)` | `TextField.make(t -> t.placeholder("Name").text(name))` | `TextField::new` (no binding yet) |
| `Toggle("On", isOn: $on)` | `Toggle("On", isOn: writable)` | `Toggle.make(t -> t.label("On").isOn(binding))` | `Toggle(style)` (no binding yet) |
| `Slider(value: $v, in: 0...100)` | `Slider(value: writable, in: min...max)` | `Slider.make(s -> s.value(vSig).min(0).max(100))` | `Slider::new` (no binding yet) |
| `DatePicker("D", selection: $d)` | `DatePicker("D", selection: writable)` | `DatePicker.make(d -> d.mode(DatePickerMode.DATE).selection(days))` | `DatePicker` (bare) |
| `.foregroundStyle(.red)` | `.foregroundStyle(Color)` | `.modifiers(foregroundStyle(f -> f.color(Color)))` | `.modifiers(ForegroundStyle(Color::argb(0xFF0000FF)))` |
| `.background(.gray)` | `.background(Color)` | `.modifiers(background(b -> b.color(Color)))` | `.modifiers(Background(Color::argb(0xFFEEEEEE)))` |
| `.border(.blue, width: 2)` | `.border(Color, width: 2)` | `.modifiers(border(b -> b.color(Color).width(2)))` | `.modifiers(Border::new(Color::argb(…), 2.0))` |
| `.frame(width: 100, height: 24)` | `.frame(width:height:alignment:)` | `.modifiers(frame(f -> f.width(100).height(24)))` | `.modifiers(Frame::new(Some(100.0), Some(24.0), None))` |
| `.padding(16)` | `.padding(16)` | `.modifiers(padding(p -> p.uniform(16)))` | `.modifiers(Padding(16.0))` |
| `.font(.system(size: 28))` | `.font(size: 28)` | `.modifiers(Font.system(28))` | `.modifiers(FontSize(28.0))` |
| `.font(.largeTitle)` | `.font(Font.largeTitle())` | `.modifiers(Font.largeTitle())` | `.modifiers(Font::large_title())` |
| `.font(.custom("Georgia", size: 20))` | `.font(Font.custom("Georgia", 20))` | `.modifiers(Font.custom("Georgia", 20))` | `.modifiers(Font::custom("Georgia", 20.0))` |
| `.fontWeight(.bold)` | `.fontWeight(FontWeight)` | `.modifiers(FontWeight.BOLD)` | `.modifiers(FontWeight(700.0))` |
| `.shadow(color:radius:x:y:)` | `.shadow(color:radius:x:y:)` | `.modifiers(shadow(s -> s.color(Color).radius(r).x(x).y(y)))` | (not yet) |
| `.onTapGesture { go() }` | `.onTapGesture(action)` | `.modifiers(tapGesture(g -> g.action(() -> go())))` | `.modifiers(TapGesture::new(\|\| go()))` |
| `if showLogin { LoginView() } else { HomeView() }` | `if/else` in a result builder | `if (showLogin.get()) return new LoginView(); return new HomeView();` in `body()` (or `View.of(() -> …)` inline) | `if`/`match` in `build()` |
| `NavigationStack { … }` | `Router` + `NavigationContainer` | `NavigationContainer.make(n -> n.router(router))` | `NavigationContainer::with(\|n\| n.router(router))` |
| `NavigationLink("Users", value:)` | `NavigationLink("label", router, to)` | `NavigationLink.make(l -> l.label("Users").router(router).to("/users"))` | `navigation_link(...)` |
| `content.modifier(Card())` | `content.modifier(Card())` | `content.modifiers(card(c -> …))` | `.modifiers(Card)` |

The three operations (`make` / `modifiers` / `children`) are the one mechanism
for construction and modification alike
([§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation),
[§5.6](#56-custom-modifiers-developer-authored)); built-in and
application-authored modifiers share the same `modifiers(...)` surface.

**Status deltas captured by this table**: the Java DSL is surface-complete with
the three operations, modifiers as values via `.modifiers(...)` (no sugar on
`View`), and styles as modifiers; **every value member carries a raw + `Signal<T>`
form** (uniform signals-first configs, so any property — layout included — can
react); the Rust DSL now exposes the surface plus
**signals** — value, computed (lazy/memoized/equality-suppressed), and effect
signals in a shared `no_std` runtime (`Signal<T>`/`WritableSignal<T>`,
`Engine::signal`/`computed`/`effect`/`read`/`set`) with text/property binding —
**two-way control bindings** (input sinks collected with
`collect_input_handlers`) and **actions** (`Button::action`), plus
**styles + environment** (a subtree `Environment` threaded through
`View::build_env`, `ButtonStyle` applied with `ViewExt::button_style`),
**structural reactivity + navigation** (`RouteTable`,
`Router`, `NavigationContainer`, `NavigationLink`), and **persisted state**
(a `StateStore` trait + `PersistentState::state` auto-load/auto-save). Both are
per-project implementation status tracked in each project's `status.md`.

---

## Conformance

- The wire footprint of every DSL element above is defined by the golden
  vectors in [CONFORMANCE.md](./CONFORMANCE.md). A new DSL element MUST add
  vectors before any implementation depends on it.
- Component ids: [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md); property ids and value
  types: [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md); event ids and listener bits:
  [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md). These specs are the single source of truth.
- The v3 authoring surface (`make` + lowercase modifier functions,
  config-with-styles, no `Mod` suffix, single-value shortcuts) is a
  **source-surface** change only: it emits the **same bytes** as the prior
  v2 `.of(...)` / `with(...)` surface for an equivalent tree — no
  component/property/event/opcode change.

# Contributing to Pathland

Thanks for your interest in Pathland — an open, cross-platform, cross-language
UI protocol. This guide covers how to build, test, and contribute.

## Code of conduct

This project is governed by the [Contributor Covenant](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). By
participating you agree to abide by its terms.

## Security

Found a vulnerability? **Do not open a public issue** — report it privately per
[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

## Project map

- `lib/rust/` — the Rust workspace: `pathland-core` (protocol), `pathland-engine`
  (emitter/signals), `pathland-view` (DSL), `pathland-core-transport`,
  `pathland-core-capi` (C ABI), `pathland-render-gtk`, `pathland-render-html`,
  `pathland-view-native`, `pathland-render-gtk-demo`.
- `lib/java/` — the Maven reactor: `pathland-view` (`com.pathland.view`),
  `pathland-view-processor`, `pathland-render-html`, `pathland-state-redis`,
  `pathland-demo-views`, the Quarkus/Spring demos, and the TypeScript DOM
  renderer (`lib/typescript`).
- `spec/` — the protocol contract: `OPCODE.md` (primary), `PRIMITIVES.md`,
  `MODIFIERS.md`, `EVENTS.md`, `CONFORMANCE.md` (golden vectors), `DSL.md`
  (authoring surface).

Implementation status per project lives in each crate/module's `status.md`.

## Prerequisites

- **Rust**: stable toolchain (`rustup`); `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target for the
  `no_std` direction guard.
- **Java**: JDK 17+ (Maven `release=17`; the whole stack runs on every LTS from 17).
- **GTK4** (Linux) for `pathland-render-gtk`.

## Build & test

```bash
# Rust workspace
cd lib/rust && cargo test

# no_std / wasm32 direction guard (requires: rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown)
cd lib/rust && ./check-wasm.sh

# C ABI (cdylib) used by Java JNA / native hosts
cd lib/rust && cargo build -p pathland-core-capi

# Java reactor (the core libraries; the Quarkus/Spring demos are excluded from
# CI but buildable with: cd lib/java && mvn -q install)
cd lib/java && mvn -q -B test -pl '!pathland-quarkus-demo,!pathland-spring-boot-demo'
```

CI runs exactly these commands (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`).

## Making changes

1. Open an issue first (or pick an open one) so the work is visible. Issues are
   labelled by epic: `hardening`, `benchmarking`, `tooling`, `a11y-seo`,
   `packaging`, and grouped into milestones `1 · Hardening & Memory Safety`
   through `5 · Packaging & Grant Readiness`.
2. Create a focused branch (`fix/…`, `feat/…`, `docs/…`).
3. Keep changes small and reviewable; add/update tests with every change.
4. Update the relevant `status.md` file when you land protocol or renderer work
   (the specs describe the contract; implementation status lives in `status.md`).
5. Keep commits atomic with clear messages (see below). No DCO sign-off is
   required.

## Commit style

- Short, imperative subject line (`feat(view): …`, `fix(transport): …`,
  `docs(spec): …`, `refactor(…): …`).
- Follow the repo's existing history as the style guide.
- Reference the issue where useful (`Fixes #NN`).

## Protocol changes (important)

- Update `spec/OPCODE.md` **first**, plus the affected companion catalog and the
  golden vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` **before** implementations depend on
  the change.
- Keep the 16-byte opcode format stable; wire-format changes must bump the
  `version` field (currently 1) per `spec/OPCODE.md`.
- New components/properties: allocate IDs in the specs + `constants.rs`
  (`lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs`), then mirror across
  `lib/java/…/Components.java`/`Properties.java` and `lib/typescript/src/constants.ts`,
  and update each renderer + its `status.md`.

## Non-negotiable principles

- Renderers are **stateless pure functions** of the opcode stream.
- The engine emits **structure + constraints**, never positions/rects.
- Emission is **diff-based**: only changed nodes emit; unchanged trees emit zero
  opcodes.
- Binary both ways: tree mutations (app → renderer) and raw-input events
  (renderer → app) share the 16-byte opcode format.

## Communication

- Issues/PRs are the primary channel.
- Contact the maintainers at `michael@apaq.dk` for private matters.---GENAI---
# Generative AI transparency

Pathland is a **human-directed** engineering project. This statement documents how
generative AI is used in its development, in line with the [NLnet Restack GenAI
policy](https://nlnet.nl/foundation/policies/generativeAI/).

## How AI is used

- **Design decisions are human.** The architectural choices — the fixed-size ring
  buffer and 16-byte opcode slot, "declarative, not positioned", renderer
  statelessness, signal-based diff emission, the single opcode format for both
  directions, the specification and conformance vectors, and the choice of the
  first DSLs (Rust + Java) — were made and steered by the maintainer. The spec
  (`spec/`) is the authority and **locks in** accepted decisions.
- **AI assists with implementation and drafting.** Most code, tests, and
  documentation were drafted with generative-AI assistance under the maintainer's
  direction and then reviewed, validated, and integrated by the maintainer.
  Tools used: **Gemini** (high-level design brainstorming, reasoning about
  technical approaches) and **DeepSeek v4.0 Flash / Pro** (code and document
  assistance).
- **Human accountability.** The maintainer understands and can explain the design
  and code decisions, and is responsible for correctness, clarity, and
  reproducibility. AI output is never merged unexamined.

## Contribution policy

- All code is contributed under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE) and must be
  original or compatible with that license (AI-assisted contributions must not
  reproduce copyrighted or incompatible material).
- If you use AI assistance in a pull request, say so in the PR description and
  ensure a human has reviewed and understood the contribution before submitting.

## Provenance

Prompt-provenance logs for the code and grant-drafting sessions are available on
request (opencode session exports; a best-effort summary of the Gemini
discussions). See also [`docs/GRANT.md`](docs/GRANT.md) §13 and
[`docs/NLNET-APPLICATION.md`](docs/NLNET-APPLICATION.md).

questions.question: How should the Kotlin DSL relate to the existing Java library?

options.label: Kotlin facade over pathland-view (Recommended)
options.description: New Kotlin module depends on the Java DSL/emitter/signals/wire codec. Idiomatic Kotlin builders wrap the Java primitives. Reuses all protocol behavior and guarantees byte-identical output.

options.label: Independent Kotlin implementation
options.description: Reimplement the emitter, signals, and wire codec in Kotlin. Much larger, duplicates the reference implementation, higher risk of drift.

options.label: Kotlin Multiplatform core
options.description: Build a KMP (JVM + JS/native) DSL. Significant build/tooling work; no Gradle or KMP setup exists in the repo today.

questions.question: Where should the Kotlin library live and build?

options.label: lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin, Maven reactor (Recommended)
options.description: Adds a Kotlin module to the current Maven reactor, reuses parent dependency management, and is covered by `cd lib/java && mvn test` in CI with no workflow change.

options.label: lib/kotlin/pathland-view-kotlin, separate Maven build
options.description: Keeps Kotlin physically separate, but needs its own parent/POM wiring and a CI update to run its tests.

options.label: Gradle module under lib/kotlin
options.description: More natural Kotlin tooling, but introduces a second build system alongside Maven.

questions.question: How should persisted `State<T>` work for Kotlin views?

options.label: Kotlin delegate + base class (Recommended)
options.description: `val count by state(0)` auto-keys by property name, backed by a Kotlin base view that binds to the session's PersistentState at render. No kapt, no annotation processor, works on all JDKs.

options.label: kapt + existing Java processor
options.description: Use @JvmField State fields and run pathland-view-processor via kapt. Matches Java exactly but adds kapt fragility across JDK 17/21/25.

options.label: Explicit state wiring only
options.description: Require `State(0, "key")` and an explicit bind call. Simplest but least SwiftUI-like.

questions.question: Should Kotlin offer SwiftUI-style modifier sugar on views in addition to `.modifiers(...)`?

options.label: Yes: `.padding(8f)`, `.frame(...)`, etc. (Recommended)
options.description: Add extension functions on View that delegate to the Java Modifiers facade. `.modifiers(...)` remains available; sugar is source-only and emits identical bytes.

options.label: No: only `.modifiers(padding(8f))`
options.description: Strictly mirrors the current Java DSL and spec canonical examples, but is noticeably less SwiftUI-like.

options.label: Sugar only for the most common modifiers
options.description: Expose padding/frame/foregroundStyle/background/font/opacity sugar; leave the rest through `.modifiers(...)`.

content.text:
## Plan: Kotlin DSL (DX-first facade)

### Architecture

Build **`lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin`** as a Kotlin facade over `pathland-view`. It reuses the Java emitter, signals, wire codec, navigation, and renderers, so Kotlin-authored trees are **byte-identical** to equivalent Java trees.

Package: `dev.pathland.view.dsl` (keeps Kotlin builders separate from the Java classes, avoiding `Text`/`VStack` class-vs-function clashes when users import only the DSL).

### DX target

```kotlin
import dev.pathland.view.View
import dev.pathland.view.dsl.*

class CounterView : KotlinView() {
    private var count by state(0)          // auto-keyed "count", no processor

    override fun body(): View = VStack(spacing = 8f) {
        Text("Count: $count")
        HStack(spacing = 4f) {
            Button("−") { count-- }
            Button("+") { count++ }
        }
    }.padding(16f)
}
```

Key ergonomics:
- `Text("…")`, `VStack { … }`, `Button("Save") { save() }` — SwiftUI-shaped names.
- Trailing blocks auto-collect children: no `.children(...)` boilerplate.
- `.padding(16f)`, `.frame(width = …)`, `.foregroundStyle(…)`, `.onTapGesture { … }` — modifier sugar, not `.modifiers(padding(…))`.
- `signal(0)`, `computed { … }`, `effect { … }`, `sig.value`, `Signal<T>.map { … }`.
- `if` / `when` / `for` inside `body()`.
- `ForEach(items) { item, index -> … }` with row auto-collection.
- `val router = navigator("/") { route(...) }`, `NavigationStack(router)`, `NavigationLink("Users", to = "/users")`.
- `Video(player)`, `player.attach()`.

### Key implementation choices

1. **Auto-registration via a scoped collector**
   - Top-level view functions register themselves into the current `VStack`/`HStack` block using a thread-local stack of child lists (same synchronous, single-threaded contract as the emitter).
   - `KotlinView`’s constructor also registers itself, so `VStack { CounterView() }` works without `.children(...)`.
   - Nested containers push/pop their own scope; a single-child `ForEach` row renders as that child, preserving Java byte output.

2. **Modifier sugar**
   - Extension functions on `View` delegate to the Java `Modifiers` facade.
   - Because `ViewBuilder.modifiers` mutates in place, `Text("a").padding(8)` works even though the builder was already auto-registered.
   - `.modifiers(...)` remains available as the escape hatch.
   - Provide common typed forms plus config-lambda forms for full reactive coverage.

3. **State**
   - `KotlinView` base class + `state(initial, key = null)` property delegate.
   - `provideDelegate` captures the property name for auto-keying.
   - At render, `KotlinView` binds delegates to `env.state()` (`PersistentState`), then runs `body()` in the tracked slot.
   - No kapt and no annotation processor.

4. **Signals**
   - Thin wrappers over `Signals` plus Kotlin conveniences: `.value`, `update`, `map`, `computed`, `effect`, `untracked`, `constant`.
   - Raw config values remain constants; signal values become bindings exactly as in Java.

### Modules and files

Add to `lib/java/pom.xml` modules:
```xml
<module>pathland-view-kotlin</module>
```

New module `lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin`:
- `pom.xml` — depends on `pathland-view`, Kotlin stdlib, kotlin-maven-plugin (JVM target 17), JUnit 5.
- `src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/dsl/`
  - `Signals.kt`
  - `Scope.kt` — `@PathlandDsl`, thread-local child collection.
  - `Views.kt` — Text, Image, Icon, Color, shapes, Divider, Spacer, ProgressView, Gauge, Label.
  - `Containers.kt` — VStack/HStack/ZStack, Grid/GridRow, ScrollView, Lazy*, SizeThatFits, ProxyView.
  - `Controls.kt` — Button, TextField/SecureField, TextEditor, Toggle, Slider, Stepper, DatePicker, Picker, Menu, ColorPicker.
  - `Modifiers.kt` — SwiftUI-style extensions for the full modifier surface.
  - `State.kt` — `KotlinView`, `state(...)`, delegate.
  - `Navigation.kt` — navigator, container, links, intents.
  - `Media.kt` — Video/MediaController helpers.
  - `Theme.kt` — token/theme helpers.
- `status.md` — required by `AGENTS.md`.

### Testing

New tests under `src/test/kotlin/...`:
- **Byte-identical conformance**: render the same tree authored in Kotlin and Java; compare opcode lists/frame bytes.
- Port representative Java `EmitterTest` cases: mount, `SET_TEXT`/`SET_PROPERTY` deltas, zero opcodes on unchanged recompute, two-way text/value/date routing.
- ForEach static + reactive; body branches with `if`/`when`.
- State delegate: auto-key, explicit key, persistence with `InMemoryStateStore`.
- Navigation: route swap and back/depth.
- Modifier sugar emits the same properties as `.modifiers(...)`.
- Auto-registration: nested containers, custom `KotlinView`, single-child ForEach output.

Commands:
```bash
cd lib/java && mvn -q -pl pathland-view-kotlin -am test
cd lib/java && mvn -q test          # full reactor, already run by CI
```

### Documentation updates

- `AGENTS.md`: add the Kotlin module to the Java library list, cross-language vocabulary status, and test command.
- `spec/DSL.md` §9.3.1: update the “Kotlin not implemented” gap; add the adopted Kotlin spelling/examples.
- `lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin/status.md`: implemented surface and known gaps.
- Optional: `CONTRIBUTING.md` project map and a short Kotlin usage section.

### Known tradeoffs / risks

- Users should import `dev.pathland.view.dsl.*` for builders and Java types only for enums/keys (`HorizontalAlignment`, `FontWeight`, …), avoiding class/function name ambiguity.
- Thread-local auto-registration relies on the documented single-threaded synchronous render contract; tests will cover nesting and reuse.
- Full reactive overload combinations are verbose in Kotlin; common cases get named params, uncommon combinations use config-lambda/`.modifiers(...)`.
- `KotlinView` state binding is the supported path; state read in field initializers before first render is documented as unsupported (read in `body()`).
- Kotlin compiler version must be verified against the CI JDK 17/21/25 matrix.

### First milestone

Scaffold the module and land:
1. signals + scope auto-registration,
2. `Text`/`VStack`/`HStack`/`Button` + core modifier sugar,
3. `KotlinView` + `state`,
4. conformance tests proving byte-identical output.

Then fill in the remaining primitives, controls, modifiers, navigation, and media.

# pathland-view-kotlin — implementation status

**Last updated:** October 30, 2026

The idiomatic Kotlin authoring surface (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`). A thin facade over
the Java `pathland-view` DSL, signals, emitter, and wire codec, so Kotlin-authored
trees emit byte-identical opcodes.

## Implemented

- **SwiftUI-shaped builders**: `Text`, `Image`, `Icon`, `Color`, `Rectangle`,
  `Circle`, `Ellipse`, `Capsule`, `RoundedRectangle`, `Shape`, `Divider`, `Spacer`,
  `ProgressView`, `Gauge`, `Label`, `Group`.
- **Containers**: `VStack`, `HStack`, `ZStack`, `Grid`, `GridRow`, `ScrollView`,
  `LazyVStack`, `LazyHStack`, `LazyVGrid`, `LazyHGrid`, `ViewThatFits`/`Fit`,
  `ProxyView`.
- **Controls**: `Button` (title or label subtree), `TextField`, `SecureField`,
  `TextEditor`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`, `DatePicker`, `Picker`, `Menu`,
  `ColorPicker`.
- **Automatic child collection**: `VStack { Text("a"); Text("b") }` needs no
  `.children(...)`. A custom `KotlinView` constructed inside a block auto-registers.
  An explicit `view.add()` / `+view` is available for Java-constructed views (e.g.
  `mediaController.attach()`).
- **Signals**: `signal`, `computed`, `constant`, `effect`, `untracked`,
  `Signal<T>.value`, `WritableSignal<T>.value`, `Signal<T>.map`, `readonly`.
- **Modifier sugar**: `.padding`, `.frame`, `.offset`, `.position`, `.fixedSize`,
  layout priority/z-index/aspect ratio, the full text-formatting surface,
  foreground/background/border/corner radius/shadow, visual effects, transforms,
  visibility/disabled/hit-testing, accessibility, tap/pointer events,
  environment binding, styles, window metadata, and navigation intents. The
  Java `.modifiers(...)` operation remains available as an escape hatch.
- **Persisted state**: `KotlinView` base class + `val count by state(0)`
  (auto-keyed by property name) or `state(0, "key")`; a `mutableState(0)` signal
  form for two-way controls. Bound to the session's `PersistentState` before the
  first `body()` render — no kapt and no annotation processor.
- **Reactive bodies**: plain `if`/`when`/`for` in `body()`; `ForEach` over a static
  list or `Signal<List<T>>` with row-scoped child collection.
- **Navigation**: `navigator { route(...) }`, `NavigationStack`, `NavigationLink`,
  `isActive`, and `.navigate`/`.push`/`.replace` intents.
- **Media**: `Video(controller)`; audio remains view-less (`controller.attach()`
  can be added with `+`).
- **Tests**: byte-identical Kotlin-vs-Java frame comparison, auto-collection,
  modifier property parity, fine-grained signal deltas, persisted/stateful bodies,
  reactive `ForEach`, two-way `TextField`, navigation swaps and link intents.

## Not implemented / gaps

- Reactive **layout value** combinations that need several signals at once are
  available through the Java config builders (`Grid.make { ... }`); the Kotlin
  named-argument overloads cover raw values plus the common single-signal cases.
- A Kotlin-native annotation processor is intentionally not used. `state(...)`
  works on `KotlinView` subclasses; a plain `View` implementation should use
  signals directly or extend `KotlinView`.
- No Kotlin Multiplatform target yet — the module is JVM-only over the Java
  library.
- `SecureField` is implemented in the Kotlin facade (`TEXT_FIELD` + `IS_SECURE`)
  because the Java `TextField.Config` does not yet expose `secure`.

The reusable Java library set (`dev.pathland`, Maven reactor, Java 17+) — the same
hand-written DSL serves Spring Boot, Quarkus, and desktop apps:

```
lib/java/
  pathland-view/        # com.pathland.view — SwiftUI-like DSL (View/VStack/Text/Button/
                        #   ButtonStyle via a thread-local Environment), Angular-style
                        #   signals/computed/effects (com.pathland.view.signal), fine-grained
                        #   emitter with node-level binding effects (com.pathland.view.emit),
                        #   wire codec (com.pathland.view.transport), lazy JNA ring interop
                        #   (com.pathland.view.ffm), cross-platform state
                        #   (com.pathland.view.state: StateStore/PersistentState/State)
  pathland-view-processor/ # JSR 269 annotation processor: generates <View>_StateBinder
                        #   for State fields (auto-keyed by field name)
  pathland-render-html/ # com.pathland.render.html — JNA shim over the Rust HTML
                        #   renderer (libpathland_render_html): one renderer, every language.
                        #   The jar embeds the Rust cdylib (META-INF/native/) so it's
                        #   self-contained. The dylib is built by CI's rust job and handed
                        #   to java via an artifact; locally, `cargo build -p

                        #   step fails loudly if it's missing).
  pathland-state-redis/ # com.pathland.state.redis — Lettuce RedisStateStore
  pathland-server-core/ # com.pathland.server — transport-agnostic server runtime:
  `ForEach.of(list | Signal<List<T>>, (item, index) -> View)` is the reactive
  list component (static lists may use streams/`for` directly).
  `NavigationContainer` / `SizeThatFits` are ordinary components. The root
  component type must stay stable across re-renders. (Rust parity is Phase 2.)
- **Cross-language vocabulary** (spec DSL.md §9.3.1): the same anchors across
  Swift, Java, Kotlin, Rust, and TypeScript — `View`, `body`/`build`, `Signal`,
  `computed`, `State`, `ForEach`, `View.of`, `children`, `modifiers`. Use native
  control flow (`if`/`switch` in Swift/Java, `if`/`when` in Kotlin, `if`/`match`
  in Rust, ternary/`switch` in TypeScript); Java uses `View.of` only where an
  inline expression is needed. Swift is the canonical SwiftUI-shaped reference;
  Kotlin/Swift are not implemented yet and Rust parity is Phase 2.
- **The three operations (spec DSL.md §2)**: every concrete view exposes
  `make(...)` (values — the only static; `make(Consumer<Config>)`, `make(value)`,
  `make()`), and the instance operations `.modifiers(ViewModifier...)` and
  `.children(View...)` chain on the returned builder. Java's static-vs-instance
  rule means the statics sit on the view class, the chain on the builder; a bare
The semantic surface is catalogued in the companion specs: **`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`**
(primitive views + component IDs), **`spec/MODIFIERS.md`** (core modifiers = the
`PARAMETER` properties), **`spec/EVENTS.md`** (core events + listener bits),
**`spec/LAYOUT.md`** (frame & layout allocation contract). The
tables below are a quick recap of the protocol surface; the companion files
carry the authoritative ID allocations.

> **Implementation status lives in each project's `status.md`**, not in the
> specs: `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/status.md`,
> `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-gtk/status.md`,

> `lib/java/pathland-view/status.md`, `lib/java/pathland-render-html/status.md`,
> and the other Rust crates' `status.md` files.

### Opcode Format

Every opcode is exactly 16 bytes:

```
[Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]

content.text:
Implemented the Kotlin DSL as `lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin` (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`), a DX-first facade over the Java DSL/emitter/signals.

What landed:
- SwiftUI-shaped builders: `Text("…")`, `VStack(spacing = 8) { … }`, `Button("Save") { … }`, controls, grids, lazy stacks, `ViewThatFits`, `ProxyView`.
- Auto child collection, including inline custom `KotlinView`s; field subviews use `+child`.
- SwiftUI modifier sugar: `.padding(16)`, `.frame(width = 100)`, `.foregroundStyle(...)`, `.onTapGesture { ... }`, etc.
- Signals: `signal`, `computed`, `effect`, `.value`, `.map`; persisted state via `val count by state(0)`.
- Navigation/media helpers, `SecureField`, reactive `ForEach`, and `if`/`when` bodies.
- Tests cover byte-identical Kotlin-vs-Java output, auto-collection, modifiers, signal deltas, persisted state, `ForEach`, two-way `TextField`, navigation, and `SecureField`.

Docs/status updated in `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `spec/DSL.md`, and `lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin/status.md`.

Verification:
- `cd lib/java && mvn -q clean test` passes.
- Kotlin module also passes on JDK 25.
- `mvn -q -P release -pl pathland-view-kotlin -am package -DskipTests` passes.
Good... I am wondering though, if the ergonmics would be even better if we created a full kotlin implemementation instead of just a facade?
I’ll assess where the facade actually constrains ergonomics versus where a full Kotlin implementation would only add duplication, then lay out the realistic options.

content.text:
Short version: **a full Kotlin implementation would improve some ergonomics, but most of the remaining friction is in the authoring model and Kotlin’s language constraints — not in “Java vs Kotlin” for the emitter.** It is only worth doing if you also want Kotlin Multiplatform, no-Java dependency, or a Kotlin-owned protocol implementation.

### What a full Kotlin implementation would actually improve

| Area | Current facade | Full Kotlin potential |
|---|---|---|
| Types | Leaks Java enums/records: `FontWeight.BOLD`, `HorizontalAlignment.CENTER`, Java `Color`/`Length` | Kotlin-native enums/value classes, better defaults, null-safety; e.g. `object Bold : FontWeight` |
| Config values | Raw/signal overloads and Java `Consumer<Config>` adapters | Kotlin data-class configs, sealed `Reactive<T>`, cleaner defaults and builder lambda shapes |
| State | `KotlinView` + `by state(0)` + a stack-walker to avoid field-child leakage | Native `State<T>` delegates on a Kotlin `Component`, no base-class/stack trick |
| Component model | Must implement Java `View`; `renderNode` contract leaks through | Kotlin `View`/`Component` sealed hierarchy with idiomatic `body` |
| Builders | Clever thread-local auto-collection; field subviews need `+child`; argument views can leak | Could design a stricter `ViewScope` or add a compiler plugin for true result-builder-like semantics |
| Signals | Java interface + Kotlin extension sugar | Rich Kotlin API: operator access, delegates, `Flow` interop, typed derived signals |
| Controls | `SecureField` needed a custom node because Java `TextField.Config` lacks `secure` | Natural control configs |
| Multiplatform | JVM-only | KMP common emitter/wire layer possible |

### What it would *not* magically fix

- Kotlin has **no implicit numeric conversions**, so `spacing = 8` still needs Int overloads or a `Dp` type.
- Kotlin has **no native SwiftUI result builders**; `VStack { Text("…") }` still needs a scope mechanism or a compiler plugin.
- `@State`/`@Binding` still need delegates or annotations.
- Modifier chaining still needs Kotlin extension functions.
- The current facade already emits **byte-identical opcodes**; a full implementation would not improve protocol correctness.

### The real cost

The Java protocol/authoring layer is ~5k lines across ~210 classes, including tricky behavior:
- retained-tree diffing, component slots, unique-id guards,
- `SIZE_THAT_FITS` snapshot/live downgrade,
- media controller pinning, proxy views, navigation intent resolution,
- SSR snapshot emission, window metadata, zero-opcode recomputes.

A full Kotlin stack means reimplementing the emitter, retained node model, signals, and wire codec, then maintaining a **third reference implementation** alongside Java and Rust. Every future Java/Rust bug fix would need a Kotlin parity fix. That is a large ongoing tax for ergonomic gains that are mostly achievable in the facade.

### Better intermediate: Kotlin-native authoring layer

Keep the Java emitter/wire codec, but replace the **authoring layer** with Kotlin-owned classes:

- Kotlin `View` primitives/controls backed by the same `PathlandNode`/emitter contract.
- Kotlin-native `Color`, `Length`, `Alignment`, `FontWeight`, `ToggleStyle`, `Chrome`, etc.
- A sealed `Reactive<T>` value with concise static/signal forms.
- A Kotlin `Component` base with native `by state(...)` and no `StackWalker`.
- A cleaned-up `ViewScope`/builder model; optionally a compiler plugin later for result-builder semantics.
- Keep the same conformance tests and byte-identical output.

This gets roughly **80% of the DX benefit at 20–30% of the cost**, and keeps one emitter as the source of truth.

My recommendation: **do not build a full Kotlin stack yet**. Build this Kotlin-native authoring layer first. Revisit a full implementation only if KMP, independence from Java, or a Kotlin-only protocol core becomes a product goal.

Which is the actual driver for you?

1. **Authoring DX only** → Kotlin-native authoring layer (recommended).
2. **No Java dependency / full Kotlin stack** → justify the emitter/signals reimplementation.
3. **Kotlin Multiplatform** → full or shared-core architecture; bigger design decision.
4. **Performance/zero-allocation** → a specialized Kotlin emitter could help, but the current facade is unlikely to be the bottleneck.

Lets investigate the autoring platform. Also lets consider if it would make sense to drop the java dsl in favor of kotlin dsl keeping in mind that my main audience is the jvm backend developers to begin with. content.text:
## Findings

**1. Yes — Java has a full second engine implementation, not just a DSL.**

Java `pathland-view` contains:

- **Engine / retained tree / diff**: `Emitter` (~1,000 lines), `ViewSlot`, `PathlandNode`, `Modified`, `RenderResult`, `ReactiveValues`
- **Signals**: `dev.pathland.view.signal.*`
- **Wire protocol**: `Opcode`, `ProtocolFrame`, `FrameCodec`, `ValueEncoder`, `OpcodeSink`, `FrameOpcodeSink`
- **Protocol constants**: `Components`, `Properties`, `Commands`, `Categories`, `ValueTypes`
- **State**: `State`, `PersistentState`, `StateStore`
- **Events / environment**: `Event`, `EnvironmentData`, `InputDispatcher`, `Environment`

Rust has the same responsibilities in `pathland-core`, `pathland-engine`, `pathland-view`, and `pathland-core-transport`. So Java is a **parallel implementation of the engine**, with its own retained-tree diff and signal runtime. Feature drift is already visible: Java has proxy views and SSR snapshot-fit behavior; Rust has a different retained-tree/snapshot model and zero-allocation focus.

**2. Some Java code is protocol-layer duplication that should be generated or specified centrally.**

Definitely shareable/generatable:

- `Components`, `Properties`, `Commands`, `Categories`, `ValueTypes` → hand-mirrored today; Rust is the canonical source. TypeScript already generates constants from Rust (`pathland-ts-codegen`). Java/Kotlin should do the same.
- Enum codes for alignment, shape kind, text style, roles, listeners, etc. → same story.
- Golden wire vectors and event/frame encodings → already partly tested, but should be cross-language conformance suites.

Harder but still protocol-level:

- `Opcode`/`ProtocolFrame`/`FrameCodec`/`ValueEncoder` → wire semantics are protocol, but the implementation is language-specific. A pure JVM wire codec is valuable for Spring/Quarkus. Sharing code would require native/WASM; probably not worth it for backend.
- `Emitter`/signals/state → these are algorithm implementations, not wire. They could be shared through a Rust C ABI/WASM engine, but that would make JVM backends depend on a native library or WASM runtime. For a JVM-backend-first audience, keeping a pure JVM engine is likely more important than eliminating duplication.

**3. Authoring is the layer that should remain language-specific.**

The DSL, `State` wiring, annotation processor, Kotlin delegates, environment scoping, and builder ergonomics are host-language concerns. They should not be “shared with Rust”; they should be specified behaviorally and implemented per language.

**4. Dropping the Java DSL is probably premature.**

- 243 Java source files currently import `dev.pathland.view`.
- The Spring Boot and Quarkus demos/starters are Java-first.
- Kotlin DSL top-level functions and default arguments do not map cleanly back into Java (`DslKt.VStack(...)`, no trailing lambdas, no named arguments), so Java users would lose ergonomics.
- Your stated audience is JVM backend developers — that includes both Java and Kotlin teams.
- A Kotlin-only direction is viable, but it implies either dropping Java-first users or maintaining a generated Java facade anyway.

A better strategy: **split the JVM engine from the authoring DSL**, make Kotlin a first-class/recommended authoring surface, and keep Java DSL supported. Retire Java DSL later only if usage justifies it.

## Recommended platform direction

1. **Extract a JVM engine module** (e.g. `pathland-view-core`) containing emitter, retained tree, signals, transport, state, environment, and input routing.
   - `pathland-server-core` depends only on this engine.
   - `pathland-view` (Java DSL) depends on it.
   - `pathland-view-kotlin` depends on it.
   - This enables evolving or even retiring the Java DSL without touching the server/runtime.

2. **Build the Kotlin-native authoring layer on that engine** — Kotlin value types, enums, `Reactive<T>`, `Component`/state model, typed builders. Keep the existing engine, not a duplicate emitter.

3. **Generate protocol constants for Java/Kotlin from Rust**, like TypeScript, and add engine-behavior conformance vectors.
   - This removes the worst drift risk cheaply.
   - It does not require sharing the emitter.

4. **Decide the Java DSL’s long-term role** only after Kotlin adoption data exists:
   - first-class Java + first-class Kotlin (recommended now),
   - Kotlin-first, Java supported/frozen,
   - Kotlin-only with a generated Java facade.

5. **Only consider a shared Rust engine via C ABI/WASM** if KMP, a single engine, or native/JVM parity becomes a stronger goal than pure-JVM deployment simplicity.

A few decisions will determine the concrete plan:

questions.question: What is the intended long-term role of the Java DSL?

options.label: Keep Java first-class alongside Kotlin (Recommended)
options.description: Keep both authoring surfaces; split the engine so they share it. Preserves the Java backend audience and existing demos/starters.

options.label: Kotlin-first, Java supported/frozen
options.description: New features and docs target Kotlin; Java keeps working but receives only fixes. Still requires maintaining the Java engine and DSL.

options.label: Retire the Java DSL
options.description: Port demos/starters to Kotlin and provide a Java-friendly core or generated facade. Largest migration, but possible if the audience is Kotlin-heavy.

questions.question: How should the JVM engine relate to the Rust engine?

options.label: Pure JVM engine + shared spec/conformance (Recommended)
options.description: Keep a pure Java/Kotlin engine for backend deployment. Share constants via codegen and behavior via specs/golden vectors.

options.label: Shared Rust engine via native/WASM
options.description: One engine implementation for all languages, but JVM backends take a native/WASM dependency and deployment complexity.

options.label: Evaluate both before deciding
options.description: Prototype the module split and shared-engine bridge, then compare deployment and maintenance costs.

questions.question: What should I design in detail next?

options.label: Engine/DSL module split + Kotlin authoring layer (Recommended)
options.description: Concrete package/module boundaries, dependency graph, and a Kotlin-native authoring API that keeps the shared JVM engine.

options.label: Protocol codegen + conformance plan
options.description: Generate Java/Kotlin constants from Rust and define engine conformance vectors to control cross-language drift.

options.label: Java DSL retirement/migration plan
options.description: Analyze porting demos/starters, Java interop, and whether a generated Java facade is viable.

options.label: Full Kotlin implementation plan
options.description: Plan a standalone Kotlin engine/wire implementation, including KMP considerations and parity costs.
